# How to use this guide

Pharmacology I is a learning-by-classification subject. Almost every exam answer follows the same shape: definition → classification with examples → mechanism → actions → uses → adverse effects → contraindications or interactions. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, write each classification table once from memory, draw the key diagrams (dose–response curves, G-protein pathways, catecholamine synthesis, ANS organisation), then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly; no unit has been split or joined.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with classification, mechanism and a diagram.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Introduction and pharmacokinetics | Routes of administration, agonist and antagonist types, tolerance/tachyphylaxis/idiosyncrasy, absorption and bioavailability, plasma protein binding, phase I/II metabolism, enzyme induction and inhibition, first- and zero-order kinetics |
| 2 Pharmacodynamics and drug development | Receptor classification and G-protein signalling, dose–response curve and therapeutic index, factors modifying drug action, ADRs, drug interactions, phases of clinical trials, pharmacovigilance |
| 3 Peripheral nervous system | Cholinergic and adrenergic transmission, classification and uses of cholinergics, anticholinergics, sympathomimetics and blockers, organophosphate poisoning, neuromuscular blockers, local anaesthetics, myasthenia gravis and glaucoma |
| 4 CNS part 1 | GABA and glutamate, general anaesthetics and stages, pre-anaesthetic medication, benzodiazepines vs barbiturates, antiepileptics, ethanol and methanol, disulfiram |
| 5 CNS part 2 | Antipsychotics and their side effects, antidepressant classes, lithium, levodopa with carbidopa, Alzheimer's drugs, morphine actions and poisoning, drug dependence |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Start with a one-line definition, then a **classification table with two examples per class**. Examiners give a large share of marks for a clean classification.
2. For a drug essay use the fixed order: mechanism, pharmacological actions system by system, uses, adverse effects, contraindications, interactions.
3. Draw what can be drawn: ANS outflow, cholinergic and adrenergic synapse, catecholamine synthesis pathway, G-protein cycle, log dose–response curves with antagonists, first- vs zero-order plots, GABA-A receptor with its binding sites.
4. Write drug names in full and correctly (no brand names). Underline the drug of choice where one exists (adrenaline in anaphylaxis, ethosuximide in absence seizures, naloxone in opioid poisoning, atropine plus pralidoxime in organophosphate poisoning).
5. Poisoning questions (organophosphate, atropine, barbiturate, morphine, methanol) are favourites: give features, mechanism and stepwise treatment.
6. Comparisons score well in short answers: competitive vs non-competitive antagonism, depolarising vs non-depolarising blockers, BZD vs barbiturate, typical vs atypical antipsychotics, first- vs zero-order kinetics, physical vs psychological dependence.
7. Doses are given only where they are standard and well known; for everything else, give mechanism and use rather than a number.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics with a classification table and a diagram each: **drug metabolism with enzyme induction and inhibition**, **receptor types and G-protein signalling with the dose–response curve**, **organophosphate poisoning with cholinergic and anticholinergic drugs**, **antiepileptic drugs**, and **morphine with opioid poisoning**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Key definitions in one line**

| Term | One line |
| --- | --- |
| Pharmacokinetics / pharmacodynamics | Body on drug (ADME) / drug on body (action, mechanism) |
| Bioavailability | Fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged = AUC oral / AUC IV |
| First-pass metabolism | Loss in gut wall and liver before systemic circulation (GTN, lignocaine, propranolol, morphine) |
| Volume of distribution | Amount in body ÷ plasma concentration |
| Half-life | Time for plasma level to halve; t½ = 0.693 Vd/CL; steady state after 4–5 t½ |
| Therapeutic index | LD50/ED50; narrow in digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, warfarin |
| Potency vs efficacy | Dose needed (curve position) vs maximum effect (curve height) |
| Tachyphylaxis | Rapid tolerance, not overcome by more drug (ephedrine, tyramine) |
| Idiosyncrasy | Genetic abnormal response (primaquine in G6PD deficiency) |
| ADR | Noxious, unintended response at normal doses |
| Pharmacovigilance | Detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of ADRs (PvPI, IPC Ghaziabad) |

**Contrasts examiners like**

| Pair | Difference |
| --- | --- |
| Competitive vs non-competitive antagonist | Parallel right shift, same max vs max reduced |
| First vs zero order | Constant fraction vs constant amount per time (alcohol, high-dose phenytoin) |
| Phase I vs phase II | Add polar group (CYP450 oxidation) vs conjugation (glucuronide most common) |
| Enzyme inducers vs inhibitors | Phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin vs cimetidine, erythromycin, ketoconazole, ciprofloxacin, valproate |
| Gs / Gi / Gq | ↑cAMP (β) / ↓cAMP (α2, M2) / IP3 + DAG (α1, M1, M3) |
| Depolarising vs non-depolarising blocker | Succinylcholine (fasciculations, neostigmine worsens) vs d-tubocurarine (neostigmine reverses) |
| Ester vs amide LA | Procaine (plasma esterase, allergy) vs lignocaine (liver, longer) |
| BZD vs barbiturate | ↑ frequency vs ↑ duration of Cl− opening; flumazenil vs no antidote |
| Typical vs atypical antipsychotic | D2 block, more EPS vs D2 + 5-HT2A, less EPS, more weight gain |
| Psychological vs physical dependence | Craving vs withdrawal syndrome |

**Drugs of choice and antidotes**

| Situation | Drug |
| --- | --- |
| Anaphylactic shock | Adrenaline IM (1 in 1000) |
| Organophosphate poisoning | Atropine + pralidoxime |
| Atropine (anticholinergic) poisoning | Physostigmine (severe cases) |
| Benzodiazepine overdose | Flumazenil |
| Opioid overdose | Naloxone |
| Methanol poisoning | Ethanol or fomepizole, sodium bicarbonate, dialysis |
| Paracetamol overdose | N-acetylcysteine |
| Heparin overdose | Protamine sulfate |
| Malignant hyperthermia | Dantrolene |
| Absence seizures | Ethosuximide (or valproate) |
| Focal seizures, trigeminal neuralgia | Carbamazepine |
| Status epilepticus | IV lorazepam or diazepam |
| Myasthenia gravis | Pyridostigmine / neostigmine; edrophonium for diagnosis |
| Drug-induced parkinsonism | Central anticholinergic (trihexyphenidyl) |
| Parkinson's disease | Levodopa + carbidopa |
| Bipolar disorder (prophylaxis) | Lithium (monitor levels) |

**Classic adverse effects**

| Drug | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Chloramphenicol (newborn) | Grey baby syndrome |
| Succinylcholine | Fasciculations, hyperkalaemia, apnoea with atypical pseudocholinesterase |
| Halothane | Hepatitis, arrhythmia with adrenaline |
| Nitrous oxide (prolonged) | Megaloblastic anaemia |
| Thiopentone | Laryngospasm; porphyria |
| Phenytoin | Gum hypertrophy, hirsutism, fetal hydantoin syndrome |
| Valproate | Neural tube defects, hepatotoxicity |
| Carbamazepine | Hyponatraemia, Stevens–Johnson syndrome |
| Clozapine | Agranulocytosis |
| Haloperidol | Extrapyramidal symptoms |
| MAOIs | Cheese reaction (tyramine) |
| Lithium | Tremor, hypothyroidism, diabetes insipidus |
| Morphine | Respiratory depression, constipation, miosis |
| Prazosin | First-dose hypotension |
| β-blockers | Bronchospasm, masked hypoglycaemia |

**Pathways to draw from memory**

```text
Catecholamines: Tyrosine → L-DOPA → Dopamine → Noradrenaline → Adrenaline
Acetylcholine:  Choline + Acetyl-CoA → ACh → (AChE) → Choline + Acetate
GABA:           Glutamate → (GAD) → GABA
Ethanol:        Ethanol → (ADH) → Acetaldehyde → (ALDH; blocked by disulfiram) → Acetic acid
Methanol:       Methanol → Formaldehyde → Formic acid (acidosis, blindness)
```

**Phases of clinical trials:** 0 microdose · I healthy volunteers, safety · II patients, efficacy and dose · III large randomised, confirm · IV post-marketing surveillance.

# Introduction to experimental pharmacology

**Aim:** To study the scope, methods and ethical framework of experimental pharmacology.

> PCI notes that all laboratory techniques and animal experiments in BP408P are demonstrated by simulation software and videos. Your college may run every experiment in this course as a simulation. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ from this guide.

## Principle

Experimental pharmacology studies the action of drugs on living systems under controlled conditions. Its purpose is to find out **what a drug does, how it does it, how much is needed, and how safe it is** before it is given to people.

Experiments are of four broad kinds:

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In vivo | In the whole living animal | Rota-rod, actophotometer, MES test |
| In vitro | On isolated tissues, cells or enzymes outside the body | Isolated guinea pig ileum, receptor binding |
| Ex vivo | Tissue taken from a treated animal and then tested | Liver enzymes from rats given an inducer |
| In silico | Computer models and simulations | Simulated experiments, docking |

Main uses:

1. **Screening** of new compounds for a desired activity (for example anticonvulsant or anxiolytic).
2. **Bioassay**: measuring the potency of a drug by comparing its effect with a standard.
3. **Mechanism of action** studies using agonists and antagonists.
4. **Toxicity testing**: acute, sub-acute and chronic toxicity, LD50 and safety margins.
5. **Pharmacokinetic studies**: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.

### Ethics: the 3Rs and CPCSEA

Animal use is controlled by law and by ethics.

- **The 3Rs** (Russell and Burch, 1959):
  - **Replacement** – use non-animal methods wherever possible (cell lines, isolated tissues, simulations, videos).
  - **Reduction** – use the fewest animals that still give a reliable answer (good design, proper statistics).
  - **Refinement** – reduce pain and distress (anaesthesia, analgesia, humane end points, gentle handling).
- **CPCSEA** (Committee for the Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals) is a statutory body formed under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. It registers institutions and breeders and lays down rules for housing, care and experiments.
- Every institution using animals must have an **Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC)** that approves each protocol before any animal is used.
- For teaching, CPCSEA encourages alternatives. This is why the PCI syllabus asks for these experiments to be demonstrated by simulations and videos.

## Requirements

Lab manual, a simulation package installed on computers (for example ExPharm, used in many Indian colleges), demonstration videos, copy of the current CPCSEA guidelines, observation notebook.

## Procedure

1. Read the aims of experimental pharmacology and the four types of experiment listed above.
2. Read the 3Rs and give one example of each from this course.
3. Read the role of CPCSEA and IAEC; note what a protocol submitted to the IAEC must contain (aim, species, number of animals with justification, procedures, anaesthesia/analgesia, end points, method of euthanasia).
4. Open the simulation software and go through its menu: animal selection, drug selection, dose entry, recording screen and result screen.
5. Run one simple simulated experiment (for example drug effect on locomotor activity) and note how the screen shows observations.
6. Write a short note comparing a simulated experiment with a live animal experiment.

## Observations

Record what you saw in a table like this.

**Specimen record (illustrative entries only):**

| Experiment in this course | Type | Species | Which R is applied when it is shown by simulation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phenobarbitone sleeping time | In vivo | Mouse | Replacement |
| Ciliary motility of frog oesophagus | Ex vivo tissue | Frog | Replacement |
| Rota-rod test | In vivo | Mouse | Replacement |
| Elevated plus maze | In vivo | Rat / mouse | Replacement |

## Result

The scope of experimental pharmacology, the types of experiments and the ethical framework (3Rs, CPCSEA and IAEC) were studied, and the working of the simulation software was learnt.

## Precautions

1. Never use a live animal in a class experiment without IAEC approval.
2. Treat simulation results as a learning aid; real experiments show biological variation.
3. Enter doses and units in the software carefully (mg/kg, not mg).
4. Keep a proper written record, as you would for a real experiment.

## Viva questions

1. **Define experimental pharmacology.** The study of drug action on living systems (whole animals, tissues or cells) under controlled conditions.
2. **What are the 3Rs?** Replacement, Reduction and Refinement of animal use.
3. **What is CPCSEA?** The statutory committee under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 that controls and supervises experiments on animals in India.
4. **What is the IAEC?** The Institutional Animal Ethics Committee, which must approve every animal protocol in an institution.
5. **Difference between in vivo and in vitro?** In vivo is in the whole living animal; in vitro is on tissues or cells outside the body.
6. **Give two alternatives to animal experiments.** Computer simulations and cell or tissue cultures.
7. **What is screening?** Testing many compounds by simple tests to pick out those with a desired activity.
8. **Why are simulations preferred for teaching?** They replace animals, are repeatable and cheap, and show the expected result clearly.

# Commonly used instruments in experimental pharmacology

**Aim:** To study the construction, working and uses of instruments commonly used in experimental pharmacology.

> These instruments may be shown as real equipment, as pictures or inside simulation software. Animal use with any of them needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules; follow the 3Rs.

## Principle

Each instrument either keeps a tissue alive, records a response, or measures a change in behaviour. Knowing what each measures helps you choose the right test for a drug.

## Requirements

The instruments listed below (or their images / simulated versions), lab manual, notebook.

## Procedure

1. Study each instrument: its parts, how it works, the response it records and the drugs it is used for.
2. Draw a labelled sketch of the organ bath and kymograph.
3. Fill in the observation table.

### A. Isolated tissue set-up

```text
        aerator (air / O2)
             |
   +---------+---------+        writing lever
   |  outer water bath  |  thread   _______/
   |  (thermostat)      |---------o
   |  +-------------+   |          \  writing point on
   |  | inner organ |   |             smoked drum
   |  | tube: tissue|   |
   |  | in PSS      |   |
   |  +------+------+   |
   +---------|----------+
         drain tap
```

- **Student organ bath:** an inner tube holding the tissue in a physiological salt solution (PSS), kept at a set temperature by an outer water bath and bubbled with air or oxygen. Used for isolated ileum, rectus abdominis, uterus and similar tissues.
- **Thermostat and heater:** keep the bath at the required temperature (for example about 37 °C for mammalian tissue; frog tissue is kept at room temperature).
- **Aerator:** supplies air or oxygen to the PSS.
- **Sherrington rotating drum (kymograph):** a drum covered with smoked or glazed paper that turns at a chosen speed; the lever writes the tissue's response on it.
- **Levers:** frontal writing lever (isotonic contractions of smooth muscle), Starling heart lever (frog heart). Modern labs use a force transducer and a physiograph or computer recording system instead.

### B. Behavioural and in vivo instruments

| Instrument | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Actophotometer | Locomotor activity (beam breaks by the moving animal) | CNS stimulants and depressants |
| Rota-rod | Motor coordination (time an animal stays on a turning rod) | Muscle relaxants, sedatives |
| Electroconvulsiometer | Delivers a measured electric shock | Maximal electroshock (MES) seizures |
| Eddy's hot plate / tail-flick analgesiometer | Reaction time to heat | Analgesics |
| Plethysmometer | Paw volume by fluid displacement | Anti-inflammatory drugs (paw oedema) |
| Elevated plus maze | Time and entries in open vs closed arms | Anxiolytics |
| Pole-climbing apparatus | Conditioned avoidance response | Antipsychotics |
| Metabolic cage | Separate collection of urine and faeces | Diuretics, excretion studies |

### C. Handling and dosing aids

Animal weighing balance, rodent restrainer, oral feeding (gavage) needle, insulin and tuberculin syringes, fine needles, rabbit holder, frog board and dissection set, stopwatch, centrifuge for blood samples.

## Observations

**Specimen entries (illustrative only):**

| Instrument | Animal | Setting used in the demonstration | Drug class tested | Expected effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Actophotometer | Mouse | 10 min count | CNS depressant | Lower count |
| Rota-rod | Mouse | Fixed speed set by manual | Muscle relaxant | Earlier fall |
| Electroconvulsiometer | Rat | Corneal electrodes | Antiepileptic | No tonic hind-limb extension |
| Plethysmometer | Rat | Paw volume in ml | Anti-inflammatory | Smaller rise in paw volume |

## Result

The construction, working and uses of the common instruments of experimental pharmacology were studied.

## Precautions

1. Keep the organ bath temperature and aeration steady; changes alter tissue responses.
2. Clean behavioural apparatus between animals so smell cues do not affect the next animal.
3. Check that electrodes and electrical instruments are earthed and dry.
4. Handle animals gently; stress changes behavioural results.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the use of a kymograph?** To record tissue responses on a moving drum against time.
2. **Why is the PSS aerated?** To supply oxygen and keep the tissue alive and responsive.
3. **What does an actophotometer measure?** Locomotor activity, as the number of light-beam interruptions.
4. **What does the rota-rod test?** Motor coordination; muscle relaxants make the animal fall earlier.
5. **Which instrument is used for MES seizures?** Electroconvulsiometer.
6. **What is a plethysmometer used for?** Measuring paw volume in paw-oedema models of inflammation.
7. **Name a modern replacement for the kymograph.** A force transducer with a physiograph or computer data-acquisition system.

# Study of common laboratory animals

**Aim:** To study the common laboratory animals, their features and their uses in pharmacological experiments.

> This study is done from charts, videos and simulation software. Any live animal work needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules; the 3Rs apply (prefer alternatives, use the fewest animals, avoid pain).

## Principle

Different species respond differently to drugs. A species is chosen because its body, size or sensitivity suits the test. Knowing these features explains why, for example, the guinea pig is used for histamine studies and the rabbit for eye and pyrogen studies.

## Requirements

Charts or videos of laboratory animals, simulation software, notebook.

## Procedure

1. Study each animal: scientific name, common strains, approximate adult weight used in experiments, special features and uses.
2. Note how each animal is held and identified (ear punch, ear tag, picric acid marks on fur, cage cards).
3. Fill in the table below from your study.

### Main animals

| Animal | Scientific name | Common strains | Special features | Main uses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mouse | *Mus musculus* | Swiss albino | Small, cheap, breeds fast, needs little drug | Acute toxicity (LD50), screening of CNS drugs, analgesics, anticonvulsants |
| Rat | *Rattus norvegicus* | Wistar, Sprague-Dawley | No gall bladder; cannot vomit; good size for blood sampling and surgery | Toxicity, anti-inflammatory and anti-ulcer tests, behaviour, isolated tissues |
| Guinea pig | *Cavia porcellus* | Dunkin-Hartley | Cannot make its own vitamin C; very sensitive to histamine | Anaphylaxis, bronchospasm, isolated ileum, local anaesthetic (intradermal wheal) |
| Rabbit | *Oryctolagus cuniculus* | New Zealand white | Large ear veins; large eyes; fever response to pyrogens | Pyrogen test, eye experiments, local anaesthetics on cornea, isolated intestine |
| Frog | Indian bull frog (now *Hoplobatrachus tigerinus*) | – | Cold-blooded; tissues survive at room temperature | Isolated heart, rectus abdominis, ciliary motility (mostly replaced by simulations) |
| Hamster | *Mesocricetus auratus* | Syrian | Cheek pouches | Some infection and cancer studies |

Larger animals such as dogs, cats and monkeys are used only in special studies with strict permissions, and not for undergraduate teaching.

### Approximate biological data

Values vary with strain and source; use them as rough guides only.

| Feature | Mouse | Rat | Guinea pig | Rabbit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Usual weight used in experiments | 20–30 g | 150–250 g | 300–500 g | 1.5–2.5 kg |
| Gestation | about 3 weeks | about 3 weeks | about 9–10 weeks | about 1 month |
| Typical life span | 2–3 years | 2–3 years | 5–6 years | 5–8 years |

## Observations

**Specimen entries (illustrative only):**

| Experiment | Animal chosen | Reason for the choice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phenobarbitone sleeping time | Mouse | Small, low drug need, easy to observe righting reflex |
| Effect of drugs on the eye | Rabbit | Large, unpigmented eye in albino animals; pupil easy to see |
| Intradermal wheal for local anaesthetics | Guinea pig | Skin twitches clearly on pin prick |
| Elevated plus maze | Rat | Standard model of anxiety-like behaviour |

## Result

The common laboratory animals, their special features and their uses in experimental pharmacology were studied.

## Precautions

1. Hold each animal by the method suited to it (a mouse by the tail base and scruff, a rabbit by the scruff with its hind quarters supported – never by the ears).
2. Use animals of the same strain, sex range, age and weight range in one experiment.
3. Allow animals to settle in the lab before testing.
4. Follow CPCSEA rules for every live animal.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the mouse used for LD50 studies?** It is small, cheap, breeds fast and needs very little drug.
2. **Which laboratory animal has no gall bladder?** The rat.
3. **Why is the guinea pig used for anaphylaxis studies?** It is very sensitive to histamine and develops strong bronchospasm.
4. **Which animal is used for the pyrogen test?** The rabbit.
5. **Which vitamin must be added to the guinea pig's diet?** Vitamin C, because it cannot make it.
6. **Name two rat strains.** Wistar and Sprague-Dawley.
7. **Why is the rabbit used for eye experiments?** Its eye is large and the pupil of the albino rabbit is easy to watch.
8. **Why can't rats be used to test anti-emetics?** Rats cannot vomit.

# Maintenance of laboratory animals as per CPCSEA guidelines

**Aim:** To study the housing, feeding, care and record keeping of laboratory animals as laid down in the CPCSEA guidelines.

> This topic is studied from the CPCSEA guidelines, videos and, where possible, a supervised visit to the registered animal house. Always check the current CPCSEA document; values below are general guides.

## Principle

Healthy, unstressed animals give reliable results. Poor housing, noise, wrong temperature or rough handling change body functions and spoil experiments. CPCSEA, set up under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, lays down standards so that animals are kept humanely and experiments are valid. These standards put the **Refinement** part of the 3Rs into practice.

## Requirements

Copy of the current CPCSEA guidelines, animal house plan, sample record registers, cage and bedding samples (or pictures), notebook.

## Procedure

Study and note each heading below.

### 1. Registration and committees
1. The institution and every breeder supplying animals must be **registered with CPCSEA**.
2. An **IAEC** (Institutional Animal Ethics Committee) includes scientists, a veterinarian, a person from outside the institution, a socially aware non-scientist and CPCSEA nominees. It approves protocols and inspects the facility.
3. Animals are bought only from registered breeders.

### 2. Building and environment
| Factor | General practice for rodents |
| --- | --- |
| Temperature | Kept steady, about 22 ± 3 °C |
| Relative humidity | About 30–70 % |
| Light | 12 h light : 12 h dark cycle |
| Ventilation | Fresh, filtered air with frequent air changes; no recirculation of dirty air |
| Noise | Kept low; no loud machines near rooms |
| Separation | Separate rooms for species, quarantine, breeding and experiments; clean and dirty corridors kept apart |

### 3. Cages and bedding
- Polypropylene or stainless-steel cages with stainless-steel grill tops; easy to clean and autoclave.
- Clean, dry, dust-free bedding (for example paddy husk or corn cob), sterilised and changed regularly.
- Not too many animals in one cage; space as per CPCSEA tables.
- Cage card on every cage: species, strain, sex, number, date of arrival, project and investigator.

### 4. Food and water
- Standard pelleted diet and clean drinking water, normally available at all times (ad libitum) unless a protocol needs fasting.
- Guinea pigs need extra vitamin C.
- Feed stored in a clean, dry, vermin-proof store.

### 5. Health care
- **Quarantine** new animals and allow an **acclimatisation** period (often about a week) before use.
- A veterinarian checks animal health; sick animals are separated and treated or humanely killed.
- Pain is controlled with anaesthetics and analgesics; humane end points are set in every protocol.

### 6. Hygiene and waste
- Regular cleaning and disinfection of rooms and cages.
- Dead animals and carcasses are disposed of by incineration or as per biomedical waste rules.

### 7. Records
Animal purchase register, breeding register, health and treatment record, experiment record, and death/disposal register.

## Observations

**Specimen animal-house record (illustrative entries only):**

| Date | Room | Temperature (°C) | Humidity (%) | Light cycle | Cages cleaned | Remarks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Day 1 | Rat room | 23 | 55 | 12:12 | Yes | All animals active |
| Day 2 | Rat room | 22 | 58 | 12:12 | Yes | One rat isolated (diarrhoea), vet informed |
| Day 3 | Mouse room | 24 | 52 | 12:12 | Yes | New batch in quarantine |

## Result

The CPCSEA requirements for registration, housing, feeding, health care, hygiene and records of laboratory animals were studied.

## Precautions

1. Wear apron, gloves, mask and cap in the animal house.
2. Do not move animals between rooms without permission.
3. Never overcrowd cages.
4. Keep records up to date; they are inspected.

## Viva questions

1. **Under which Act was CPCSEA set up?** The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960.
2. **What is quarantine?** Keeping newly arrived animals apart and under watch so that diseases are not brought into the colony.
3. **What is acclimatisation?** A period that lets animals settle to the new environment before use.
4. **What light cycle is used?** 12 h light and 12 h dark.
5. **What is ad libitum?** Free access to food and water at all times.
6. **What material is used for cages?** Polypropylene or stainless steel, with steel grill tops.
7. **How are carcasses disposed of?** By incineration or as per biomedical waste rules.
8. **Which part of the 3Rs does good housing support?** Refinement.

# Common laboratory techniques: blood withdrawal, serum and plasma separation, anaesthesia and euthanasia

**Aim:** To study the methods of blood withdrawal from laboratory animals, the separation of serum and plasma, and the anaesthetics and euthanasia methods used in animal studies.

> PCI asks for these techniques to be demonstrated by simulations and videos. On live animals they are done only by trained persons, under an IAEC-approved protocol and CPCSEA rules. Follow your manual for drug choices and doses.

## Principle

Blood samples are needed to measure drug levels, enzymes, glucose, lipids and blood cells. The method chosen depends on the species, the volume needed and whether the animal must survive. Animals must not feel pain or distress, so suitable anaesthesia is used, and at the end of a study they are killed humanely (euthanasia) by approved methods.

**Serum** is the clear fluid left after blood clots; it has no clotting factors such as fibrinogen. **Plasma** is the fluid part of blood kept from clotting by an anticoagulant; it still contains fibrinogen.

## Requirements

Capillary tubes (heparinised and plain), sample tubes (plain, EDTA, heparin, citrate), centrifuge, micropipettes, needles and syringes, restrainer, cotton, spirit, xylene or warm water for dilating tail veins, anaesthetic agents, simulation software or videos.

## Procedure

### A. Blood withdrawal

| Site | Species | Key points | Survival? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Retro-orbital plexus | Rat, mouse | Under light anaesthesia, a fine capillary is passed at the inner corner of the eye into the venous plexus; blood flows by capillary action | Yes, if done correctly; refined methods are now preferred |
| Lateral tail vein / tail snip | Rat, mouse | Warm the tail to dilate the vein; small volumes | Yes |
| Saphenous vein | Rat, mouse | Shave the leg, prick the vein, collect drops | Yes |
| Marginal ear vein | Rabbit | Dilate the vein by warming or gentle rubbing; use a fine needle | Yes |
| Cardiac puncture | Rat, mouse, rabbit | Under deep anaesthesia; large volume | No (terminal only) |

General rules: take the smallest volume that is enough; as a rough rule, no more than about 10 % of the animal's blood volume at one time (blood volume is roughly 6–8 % of body weight); allow recovery time between samples; press the site to stop bleeding.

### B. Separation of serum
1. Collect blood in a plain tube (no anticoagulant).
2. Let it stand at room temperature until it clots (about 20–30 min).
3. Centrifuge (for example about 3000 rpm for 10–15 min).
4. Pipette the clear, straw-coloured upper layer (serum) into a labelled tube.

### C. Separation of plasma
1. Collect blood in a tube containing an anticoagulant (EDTA, heparin or sodium citrate) and mix gently by inversion.
2. Centrifuge at once.
3. Pipette the upper layer (plasma) without disturbing the buffy coat and red cells.
4. Store serum and plasma cold (refrigerated or frozen) until analysis.

### D. Anaesthetics used in animal studies

| Agent | Route | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Isoflurane | Inhalation | Fast onset and recovery; preferred where available |
| Ketamine with xylazine | Injection (i.p./i.m.) | Common combination for surgery in rodents |
| Thiopentone / pentobarbitone | Injection (i.p./i.v.) | Barbiturates; also used in overdose for euthanasia |
| Urethane | Injection | Long anaesthesia for terminal experiments only; carcinogenic, handle with care |
| Diethyl ether | Inhalation | Old method; irritant and highly flammable, now discouraged |

Check depth of anaesthesia by loss of the pedal (toe-pinch) reflex and the righting reflex; watch breathing and keep the animal warm.

### E. Euthanasia
Acceptable methods (as per CPCSEA, chosen for species and purpose) include an overdose of a barbiturate, carbon dioxide in a properly controlled chamber, and physical methods such as cervical dislocation of small rodents done only by trained persons. Confirm death by absence of heartbeat, breathing and corneal reflex. Dispose of carcasses by incineration. Methods causing distress, such as drowning, are never acceptable.

## Observations

**Specimen readings (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Animal | Site | Volume taken (ml) | Tube | Clotting time allowed | Centrifugation | Product | Appearance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rat 1 | Retro-orbital | 0.5 | Plain | 25 min | 3000 rpm, 10 min | Serum | Clear, straw-coloured |
| Rat 2 | Retro-orbital | 0.5 | EDTA | – | 3000 rpm, 10 min | Plasma | Clear, straw-coloured |
| Rabbit 1 | Marginal ear vein | 2.0 | Heparin | – | 3000 rpm, 10 min | Plasma | Clear, slight haemolysis (pink) – repeat |

## Result

The methods of blood collection, the separation of serum and plasma, and the anaesthetics and euthanasia methods used in animal studies were studied.

## Precautions

1. Use sharp, fine needles and the correct site to avoid injury and haemolysis.
2. Do not shake blood vigorously; it causes haemolysis.
3. Label every tube with animal number, group, time and date.
4. Check depth of anaesthesia before any painful step.
5. Use only CPCSEA-approved euthanasia methods and confirm death.

## Viva questions

1. **Difference between serum and plasma?** Serum is the fluid after clotting and has no fibrinogen; plasma is from anticoagulated blood and contains fibrinogen.
2. **Name three anticoagulants.** EDTA, heparin and sodium citrate.
3. **Which blood collection method is terminal?** Cardiac puncture.
4. **Where is blood taken in rabbits?** From the marginal ear vein.
5. **Why is ether discouraged now?** It irritates the airways and is highly flammable.
6. **Why is urethane used only for terminal experiments?** It gives long anaesthesia and is carcinogenic, so the animal is not allowed to recover.
7. **How is depth of anaesthesia checked?** By loss of the pedal (toe-pinch) and righting reflexes.
8. **Name two acceptable euthanasia methods.** Barbiturate overdose and controlled carbon dioxide exposure.

# Study of different routes of drug administration in mice and rats

**Aim:** To study the common routes of drug administration in mice and rats and to calculate the volume of drug solution to be given.

> These techniques are demonstrated by simulation and videos as per the PCI note. On live animals they need IAEC approval, trained handling and CPCSEA rules. Volumes below are general guides; follow your lab manual.

## Principle

The route decides how fast and how much of a drug reaches the blood. Intravenous gives the fastest effect and complete availability; intraperitoneal is quick and easy in rodents; oral is slowest and subject to first-pass metabolism; subcutaneous and intramuscular give slower, steadier absorption.

Dose volume is calculated from the animal's weight:

**Volume to inject (ml) = Dose (mg/kg) × Body weight (kg) ÷ Concentration (mg/ml)**

## Requirements

Mice (about 20–30 g) and rats (about 150–250 g) or simulation software, animal balance, 1 ml tuberculin/insulin syringes, fine needles (higher gauge for mice), oral feeding (gavage) needle, rodent restrainer, spirit swabs, normal saline.

## Procedure

1. Weigh each animal and calculate the volume using the formula above.
2. Hold the animal firmly but gently (mouse: tail base and loose skin of the neck; rat: around the shoulders).
3. Give the dose by the chosen route as below.

| Route | Site and method | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oral (gavage) | Ball-tipped feeding needle passed gently over the tongue into the oesophagus with the head and body in a straight line | Never force; resistance means the trachea may be entered |
| Intraperitoneal (i.p.) | Lower part of the abdomen to one side of the midline, animal held head-down so the gut moves forward | Avoid the bladder and gut; most used route in rodent practicals |
| Subcutaneous (s.c.) | Loose skin at the back of the neck or flank, lifted into a tent | Slow absorption |
| Intramuscular (i.m.) | Thigh muscles of the hind limb | Small volumes only in mice |
| Intravenous (i.v.) | Lateral tail vein, warmed to dilate it, animal in a restrainer | Fastest action; inject slowly; small volumes |
| Others | Intradermal, intracerebroventricular, topical, rectal, inhalation | Special purposes |

4. After injection, return the animal to its cage and watch for distress or leakage at the site.

A common upper guide for oral and intraperitoneal dosing in mice is about 10 ml/kg; smaller volumes are used for i.m. and i.v.

## Observations and calculation

**Worked example (illustrative values only):** a mouse weighs 25 g (0.025 kg). The dose is 10 mg/kg and the stock solution is 1 mg/ml.
Amount of drug = 10 × 0.025 = 0.25 mg. Volume = 0.25 ÷ 1 = **0.25 ml**.

**Specimen record (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Animal | Weight (g) | Dose (mg/kg) | Concentration (mg/ml) | Volume given (ml) | Route | Onset of observed effect (min) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mouse 1 | 25 | 10 | 1 | 0.25 | i.v. | 1 |
| Mouse 2 | 24 | 10 | 1 | 0.24 | i.p. | 5 |
| Mouse 3 | 26 | 10 | 1 | 0.26 | s.c. | 12 |
| Mouse 4 | 25 | 10 | 1 | 0.25 | Oral | 20 |

The order of onset in the specimen record (i.v. < i.p. < s.c. < oral) is the expected order.

## Result

The routes of administration in mice and rats were studied. The expected order of onset of action is intravenous < intraperitoneal < subcutaneous < oral.

## Precautions

1. Weigh each animal on the day of the experiment.
2. Use a fresh, sharp needle of the right size; remove air bubbles before i.v. injection.
3. Pull back the plunger slightly before i.p. injection; if blood, urine or gut contents appear, withdraw.
4. Do not exceed recommended volumes.
5. Handle gently; stress changes results.

## Viva questions

1. **Which route gives the fastest action?** Intravenous.
2. **Which vein is used for i.v. injection in mice?** The lateral tail vein.
3. **Why is the animal held head-down for i.p. injection?** So the intestines move towards the chest and are not punctured.
4. **What is an oral feeding needle?** A blunt, ball-tipped needle for giving liquids directly into the stomach.
5. **How do you calculate injection volume?** Dose (mg/kg) × weight (kg) ÷ concentration (mg/ml).
6. **Why is oral availability lower?** Because of incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver.
7. **Why is the tail warmed before i.v. injection?** To dilate the vein so it is easier to see and enter.

# Effect of hepatic microsomal enzyme inducers on phenobarbitone sleeping time in mice

**Aim:** To study the effect of pretreatment with a hepatic microsomal enzyme inducer on barbiturate-induced sleeping time in mice.

> Per the PCI note, this experiment is shown by simulation software or video. Any live version needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules; keep the number of animals to the minimum (3Rs). Use the drugs and doses in your lab manual.

## Principle

Barbiturates are broken down mainly by cytochrome P450 enzymes in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (microsomes) of liver cells. **Enzyme inducers** such as phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine and rifampicin increase the amount of these enzymes when given for a few days. A barbiturate given afterwards is metabolised faster, so its blood level falls sooner and **sleeping time becomes shorter**.

**Enzyme inhibitors** (for example cimetidine or ketoconazole) do the opposite and prolong sleeping time; some manuals add an inhibitor group for comparison.

Sleep is judged by the **righting reflex**: a mouse placed on its back normally turns over at once.

- **Onset of sleep** = time from injection to loss of righting reflex.
- **Sleeping time (duration)** = time from loss to return of righting reflex.

The syllabus names phenobarbitone as the hypnotic. Phenobarbitone is slow-acting, so many manuals use a shorter-acting barbiturate such as pentobarbitone or thiopentone on the test day to measure sleeping time; the principle is the same.

## Requirements

Mice of the same sex and similar weight, divided into groups; enzyme inducer (for example phenobarbitone), barbiturate for the test day, normal saline, syringes, balance, stopwatch, cages; or simulation software.

## Procedure

1. Divide the mice into two groups (an inhibitor group may be added).
   - **Group I (control):** normal saline daily for the pretreatment period.
   - **Group II (induced):** the enzyme inducer daily for the pretreatment period (usually several days, as in your manual).
2. On the test day, weigh every mouse and give the barbiturate intraperitoneally at the same dose to all groups.
3. Start the stopwatch at injection. Turn each mouse on its back at short intervals; note the time when it can no longer turn over (loss of righting reflex = onset).
4. Keep the mice warm and watch them; note the time when the righting reflex returns.
5. Calculate onset and duration of sleep for each mouse and the group mean.

## Observations and calculation

**Specimen readings (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Group | Mouse | Weight (g) | Onset of sleep (min) | Duration of sleep (min) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I Control (saline) | 1 | 24 | 6 | 92 |
| | 2 | 26 | 5 | 88 |
| | 3 | 25 | 6 | 95 |
| | Mean | | 5.7 | 91.7 |
| II Inducer-pretreated | 1 | 25 | 7 | 46 |
| | 2 | 24 | 8 | 41 |
| | 3 | 26 | 7 | 50 |
| | Mean | | 7.3 | 45.7 |

% decrease in sleeping time = (Control mean − Test mean) ÷ Control mean × 100
= (91.7 − 45.7) ÷ 91.7 × 100 ≈ **50 %** (specimen value).

In a real experiment, compare group means with an unpaired t-test (two groups) or one-way ANOVA (more groups).

## Result

Pretreatment with the hepatic microsomal enzyme inducer shortened the barbiturate sleeping time (specimen: by about ___ %), showing faster metabolism of the barbiturate after enzyme induction.

## Precautions

1. Use mice of the same sex, age and weight range, and fast them equally if the manual asks.
2. Give the same barbiturate dose (mg/kg) to all groups.
3. Keep sleeping mice warm; low body temperature prolongs sleep and can kill.
4. Test the righting reflex the same way for every mouse.
5. Note times exactly with a stopwatch.

## Viva questions

1. **What is enzyme induction?** An increase in the amount of drug-metabolising enzymes caused by repeated exposure to certain drugs.
2. **Name three enzyme inducers.** Phenobarbitone, rifampicin and phenytoin (also carbamazepine).
3. **Why does an inducer shorten sleeping time?** The barbiturate is metabolised faster, so its level falls below the sleep-producing level sooner.
4. **What is the righting reflex?** The reflex by which an animal placed on its back turns back onto its feet.
5. **Name an enzyme inhibitor and its effect here.** Cimetidine or ketoconazole; it prolongs sleeping time.
6. **Where are microsomal enzymes found?** In the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells.
7. **Why is pretreatment given for several days?** Induction needs new enzyme to be made, which takes days.
8. **Clinical importance of enzyme induction?** It lowers the effect of other drugs, for example rifampicin reducing the effect of oral contraceptives.
practicals.title: Effect of enzyme inducers on phenobarbitone sleeping time in mice

# Effect of drugs on ciliary motility of frog oesophagus

**Aim:** To study the effect of drugs on the ciliary movement of the frog oesophagus.

> Dissection of frogs for teaching is now discouraged and this experiment is shown by simulation or video, as the PCI syllabus notes. Any live use needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules and the 3Rs apply.

## Principle

The inner lining of the frog's mouth and oesophagus carries cilia that beat in one direction, towards the stomach, and carry mucus and small particles with them. The speed of a light particle placed on the lining is a measure of ciliary activity.

Ciliary movement is increased by cholinergic drugs (acetylcholine, pilocarpine, physostigmine) and this effect is blocked by atropine. Local anaesthetics depress ciliary movement.

**Velocity of the particle = Distance travelled ÷ Time taken**

## Requirements

Frog (or simulation software / video), pithing needle, dissection set, frog board or cork board, pins, frog Ringer solution, droppers, a light marker particle (poppy seed, small piece of cork or a grain of charcoal), ruler, stopwatch; drug solutions such as acetylcholine, atropine and a local anaesthetic (lignocaine).

## Procedure

1. Pith the frog (destroy brain and spinal cord) so it feels no pain.
2. Pin it on its back on the board. Cut through the lower jaw in the midline and open the mouth and oesophagus down to the stomach.
3. Pin the cut edges so the lining of the mouth and oesophagus lies flat and faces up. Keep it moist with frog Ringer throughout.
4. Mark two points a fixed distance apart (for example 1 cm) along the oesophagus.
5. Place the marker particle at the upper mark and note the time it takes to reach the lower mark. Repeat three times for a steady control value.
6. Put a few drops of acetylcholine on the lining, wait a short time, and repeat the timing.
7. Wash with Ringer, allow recovery, then apply atropine and repeat; then atropine followed by acetylcholine.
8. Wash again and test the local anaesthetic in the same way.

## Observations and calculation

**Specimen readings (illustrative only, not real data):** distance between marks = 1 cm.

| Treatment | Time 1 (s) | Time 2 (s) | Time 3 (s) | Mean time (s) | Velocity (cm/s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control (Ringer) | 20 | 21 | 19 | 20.0 | 0.050 |
| Acetylcholine | 12 | 13 | 12 | 12.3 | 0.081 |
| Atropine, then acetylcholine | 21 | 22 | 20 | 21.0 | 0.048 |
| Lignocaine | 35 | 38 | 37 | 36.7 | 0.027 |

## Result

Acetylcholine increased the speed of ciliary transport, atropine blocked this effect, and the local anaesthetic decreased ciliary movement (specimen values).

## Precautions

1. Pith the frog completely before dissection.
2. Keep the tissue moist with Ringer at all times; drying stops the cilia.
3. Use a particle of the same size each time and place it at the same point.
4. Wash well and allow recovery between drugs.
5. Do not touch the lining with instruments more than needed.

## Viva questions

1. **In which direction do the cilia beat?** Towards the stomach.
2. **What is the effect of acetylcholine on ciliary motility?** It increases it.
3. **How does atropine act here?** It blocks muscarinic receptors and prevents the increase caused by acetylcholine.
4. **Effect of local anaesthetics on cilia?** They depress ciliary movement.
5. **Why is frog Ringer used?** It keeps the tissue alive by matching the salts of frog body fluid.
6. **What is pithing?** Destroying the brain and spinal cord of the frog with a needle so it feels no pain.
7. **Name a clinical link of ciliary function.** Mucociliary clearance in the airways, which is reduced by smoking and some drugs.
practicals.title: Effect of drugs on ciliary motility of frog oesophagus

# Effect of drugs on rabbit eye

**Aim:** To study the effects of mydriatics, miotics and local anaesthetics on the rabbit eye.

> This experiment is shown by simulation or video as per the PCI note. A live study needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules, gentle handling and the fewest animals (3Rs). Use the drug strengths in your lab manual.

## Principle

The size of the pupil depends on two muscles of the iris:

- **Sphincter pupillae** (circular, muscarinic M3, parasympathetic) – contraction makes the pupil small (**miosis**).
- **Dilator pupillae** (radial, α1-adrenergic, sympathetic) – contraction makes the pupil large (**mydriasis**).

| Drug | Type | Pupil | Light reflex | Corneal reflex |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Atropine | Antimuscarinic | Dilated (mydriasis) | Absent | Present |
| Phenylephrine | α1 agonist | Dilated (mydriasis) | Present | Present |
| Pilocarpine | Muscarinic agonist | Constricted (miosis) | Present (sluggish) | Present |
| Physostigmine | Anticholinesterase | Constricted (miosis) | Present | Present |
| Lignocaine | Local anaesthetic | Little change | Present | Absent |

Atropine paralyses the sphincter, so the dilated pupil does not react to light. Phenylephrine contracts the dilator while the sphincter still works, so the light reflex remains. A local anaesthetic blocks the sensory nerves of the cornea, so touching it gives no blink.

Some rabbits have an enzyme (atropinesterase) that breaks down atropine, so the effect of atropine may be shorter in them.

## Requirements

Albino rabbits or simulation software, rabbit holder, torch, millimetre scale or pupillometer, cotton wisp or soft hair, droppers; eye drops of atropine, pilocarpine (or physostigmine), phenylephrine and lignocaine (commercial ophthalmic preparations).

## Procedure

1. Place the rabbit in the holder in a room with steady light.
2. Before giving any drug, record in both eyes: pupil size (mm), light reflex (shine the torch and watch for constriction), corneal reflex (touch the cornea with a cotton wisp from the side and watch for a blink), and congestion of the conjunctiva.
3. Pull down the lower eyelid of one eye to form a pouch and put in 2–3 drops of the test drug. Hold the lid closed briefly and press at the inner corner of the eye to reduce drainage into the nose. The other eye is the control.
4. Record the same signs at fixed intervals (for example 5, 10, 15 and 30 min).
5. Use a different rabbit (or a different session after full recovery) for each drug, as in your manual.

## Observations

**Specimen readings at 15 min (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Drug | Pupil before (mm) | Pupil after (mm) | Light reflex | Corneal reflex | Conjunctiva | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control eye | 6 | 6 | Present | Present | Normal | No change |
| Atropine | 6 | 10 | Absent | Present | Normal | Mydriasis with cycloplegic action |
| Phenylephrine | 6 | 9 | Present | Present | Blanched | Mydriasis (α1 agonist) |
| Pilocarpine | 6 | 3 | Present, sluggish | Present | Congested | Miosis |
| Lignocaine | 6 | 6 | Present | Absent | Normal | Corneal (surface) anaesthesia |

## Result

Atropine and phenylephrine caused mydriasis (light reflex lost with atropine, kept with phenylephrine); pilocarpine caused miosis; lignocaine abolished the corneal reflex (specimen values).

## Precautions

1. Keep the room light constant while measuring the pupil.
2. Touch the cornea from the side so the rabbit does not blink at the approaching object.
3. Do not touch the cornea with the dropper.
4. Press the inner corner of the eye after instillation to limit systemic absorption.
5. Always compare with the untreated eye.

## Viva questions

1. **What is mydriasis?** Dilatation of the pupil.
2. **Why is the light reflex lost with atropine but not with phenylephrine?** Atropine paralyses the sphincter pupillae; phenylephrine acts on the dilator and leaves the sphincter working.
3. **Name two miotics.** Pilocarpine and physostigmine.
4. **What is the corneal reflex?** A blink when the cornea is touched.
5. **Why is the corneal reflex lost with lignocaine?** It blocks the sensory nerve endings of the cornea.
6. **What is cycloplegia?** Paralysis of the ciliary muscle so the eye cannot focus for near vision; caused by atropine.
7. **Why are miotics used in glaucoma?** They open the drainage angle and increase outflow of aqueous humour.
8. **Why might atropine act briefly in some rabbits?** Some rabbits have atropinesterase, which destroys atropine.

# Effect of skeletal muscle relaxants using the rota-rod apparatus

**Aim:** To study the effect of a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant on motor coordination in mice using the rota-rod apparatus.

> Shown by simulation or video as per the PCI note. Live use needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules; screen and train animals so fewer are needed (3Rs). Use the drug and dose from your lab manual.

## Principle

The rota-rod is a horizontal rod turning at a fixed speed. A normal, trained mouse can keep walking on it for a long time. Drugs that relax skeletal muscle or impair motor coordination (for example diazepam and other benzodiazepines, or centrally acting relaxants) make the mouse lose grip and **fall off earlier**. The fall-off time before and after the drug is compared.

```text
        rotating rod (fixed speed)
   ====================================
     |  mouse  |  mouse  |  mouse  |      partitions keep
     |   lane  |   lane  |   lane  |      animals apart
   ------------------------------------
        fall-off area / trip platforms
```

**% decrease in fall-off time = (Before − After) ÷ Before × 100**

## Requirements

Rota-rod apparatus, mice, diazepam (or another centrally acting muscle relaxant), vehicle (normal saline or as suited to the drug), syringes, balance, stopwatch; or simulation software.

## Procedure

1. Switch on the rota-rod and set the speed fixed by your manual.
2. **Screening:** place each mouse on the rod. Select only mice that stay on for a set cut-off time (for example 3–5 min) in repeated trials; reject the others.
3. Record the basal fall-off time of each selected mouse.
4. Give the test drug to the test group and vehicle to the control group (usually intraperitoneally).
5. After the waiting time in your manual (for example 30 min), place each mouse on the rod again and note the fall-off time. Stop at the cut-off time if the mouse has not fallen.
6. Calculate the % decrease in fall-off time for each mouse and the group mean.

## Observations and calculation

**Specimen readings (illustrative only, not real data; cut-off 300 s):**

| Group | Mouse | Fall-off time before (s) | Fall-off time after (s) | % decrease |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control (vehicle) | 1 | 300 | 295 | 1.7 |
| | 2 | 300 | 300 | 0 |
| | 3 | 300 | 290 | 3.3 |
| Diazepam | 1 | 300 | 85 | 71.7 |
| | 2 | 300 | 110 | 63.3 |
| | 3 | 300 | 70 | 76.7 |

Mean % decrease: control about 1.7 %, diazepam about 70.6 % (specimen values).

## Result

Diazepam reduced the fall-off time on the rota-rod, showing loss of muscle tone and motor coordination (specimen: about ___ % decrease).

## Precautions

1. Use only screened, trained mice.
2. Keep the rod speed and cut-off time the same for all animals.
3. Test at the same time after dosing for every mouse.
4. Keep the rod clean and dry; a soiled rod changes grip.
5. Place a soft pad below the rod so falling mice are not hurt.

## Viva questions

1. **What does the rota-rod test measure?** Motor coordination and muscle tone.
2. **Why are mice screened first?** To use only animals that can stay on the rod, so a fall after the drug is due to the drug.
3. **Name a standard drug for this test.** Diazepam.
4. **Mechanism of diazepam's muscle relaxation?** It enhances GABA-A receptor action in the spinal cord and brain, reducing reflex muscle tone.
5. **Name a centrally acting muscle relaxant other than benzodiazepines.** Baclofen (also tizanidine, chlorzoxazone).
6. **Name a peripherally acting muscle relaxant.** d-Tubocurarine or succinylcholine (neuromuscular blockers).
7. **What else besides muscle relaxation can make a mouse fall?** Sedation or ataxia from any CNS depressant, such as alcohol.

# Effect of drugs on locomotor activity using the actophotometer

**Aim:** To study the effect of CNS depressant and CNS stimulant drugs on locomotor activity in mice using the actophotometer.

> Shown by simulation or video as per the PCI note. Live use needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules; compare each animal with itself to keep numbers low (3Rs). Use the drugs and doses in your lab manual.

## Principle

Locomotor activity is a measure of alertness. The actophotometer has light beams falling on photocells across the floor of an arena. Each time the animal moves across a beam, the beam is cut and a digital counter adds one count. The arena is usually square for rats and circular for mice.

- **CNS depressants** (diazepam, chlorpromazine, phenobarbitone) **lower** the count.
- **CNS stimulants** (caffeine, amphetamine) **raise** the count.

**% change in activity = (After − Before) ÷ Before × 100**  (negative = decrease)

## Requirements

Actophotometer, mice, a CNS depressant (for example diazepam or chlorpromazine) and, if required, a stimulant (for example caffeine), vehicle, syringes, balance, stopwatch; or simulation software.

## Procedure

1. Switch on the actophotometer and check that all beams fall on the photocells (counter steady when the arena is empty).
2. Place a mouse in the arena and record the count for a fixed time (for example 10 min). This is the basal activity.
3. Give the drug (usually intraperitoneally) and return the mouse to its cage.
4. After the waiting time in your manual (for example 30 min), place it in the arena again and record the count for the same time.
5. Repeat for each mouse and calculate the % change.

## Observations and calculation

**Specimen readings for a 10-min count (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Group | Mouse | Basal count | Count after drug | % change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Diazepam | 1 | 260 | 95 | −63.5 |
| | 2 | 240 | 88 | −63.3 |
| | 3 | 275 | 110 | −60.0 |
| Caffeine | 1 | 250 | 390 | +56.0 |
| | 2 | 230 | 360 | +56.5 |
| | 3 | 265 | 400 | +50.9 |

## Result

The CNS depressant decreased and the CNS stimulant increased locomotor activity in mice (specimen: about −62 % and +54 %).

## Precautions

1. Allow each mouse to settle in the test room before the basal count.
2. Keep the room quiet, with constant light and temperature.
3. Use the same counting time before and after the drug.
4. Clean the arena between animals.
5. Test at the same time of day; activity varies with the light–dark cycle.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the principle of the actophotometer?** The moving animal cuts light beams falling on photocells; each cut is counted.
2. **Effect of diazepam on locomotor activity?** It decreases it.
3. **Effect of caffeine?** It increases it.
4. **Why is the basal count taken?** Each animal serves as its own control.
5. **Shape of the arena for mice and rats?** Circular for mice, square for rats.
6. **Why should the room be quiet?** Noise and disturbance change the animal's activity.
7. **Mechanism of caffeine's stimulant action?** Blockade of adenosine receptors in the brain.
practicals.title: Locomotor activity using the actophotometer

# Anticonvulsant effect of drugs by the MES and PTZ methods

**Aim:** To study the anticonvulsant effect of drugs against maximal electroshock (MES) seizures and pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced seizures in rats or mice.

> Shown by simulation or video as per the PCI note. Seizure models cause distress, so live use needs strict IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules, the fewest animals and humane end points (3Rs). Use drugs and doses from your lab manual.

## Principle

### A. Maximal electroshock (MES) – model of generalised tonic-clonic seizures
An electric current is passed through corneal or ear electrodes from an electroconvulsiometer. A commonly used setting is 150 mA for 0.2 s in rats and 50 mA for 0.2 s in mice. The seizure has these phases:

```text
 tonic flexion → tonic extensor (hind limbs stretched back) → clonus → stupor → recovery (or death)
```

**Abolition of the tonic hind-limb extensor phase** (or a clear cut in its duration) is taken as protection. **Phenytoin** is the standard drug; phenobarbitone, carbamazepine and valproate also protect.

### B. Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ) – model of absence and myoclonic seizures
PTZ is a GABA-A receptor antagonist. Given by injection, it produces clonic jerks and convulsions. Delay in onset of clonic seizures, fewer or no seizures, and survival show protection. **Diazepam** (also ethosuximide, valproate, phenobarbitone) protects. **Phenytoin does not protect against PTZ seizures**, which matches its clinical lack of effect in absence seizures.

## Requirements

Electroconvulsiometer with corneal or ear-clip electrodes, saline for wetting electrodes, PTZ solution, phenytoin, diazepam, vehicle, syringes, balance, stopwatch, observation cages; or simulation software.

## Procedure

### A. MES method
1. Weigh the animals and divide them into control and test groups.
2. Give vehicle to the control group and phenytoin to the test group (usually intraperitoneally); wait for the time in your manual (for example 30 min).
3. Wet the electrodes with saline and apply them to the corneas (or ears).
4. Pass the current at the setting fixed in the manual.
5. Record the duration (s) of each phase: flexion, extensor, clonus, stupor; note recovery or death.

### B. PTZ method
1. Give vehicle to the control group and diazepam to the test group; wait for the time in your manual.
2. Inject PTZ to all animals as in the manual.
3. Watch each animal in a separate cage for a fixed period (for example 30 min).
4. Record onset (latency) of the first clonic jerk, number of clonic convulsions, occurrence of tonic seizure, and death or survival.

## Observations

**Specimen readings – MES, rats (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Group | Rat | Flexion (s) | Extensor (s) | Clonus (s) | Stupor (s) | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | 1 | 3 | 12 | 14 | 70 | Recovered |
| | 2 | 2 | 11 | 16 | 65 | Recovered |
| Phenytoin | 1 | 4 | 0 | 10 | 30 | Protected |
| | 2 | 3 | 0 | 12 | 28 | Protected |

**Specimen readings – PTZ, mice (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Group | Mouse | Onset of clonic jerks (s) | Number of clonic convulsions | Tonic seizure | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | 1 | 90 | 5 | Yes | Died |
| | 2 | 110 | 4 | Yes | Recovered |
| Diazepam | 1 | No seizure in 30 min | 0 | No | Protected |
| | 2 | 1100 | 1 | No | Protected |

% protection = Number of animals protected ÷ Number tested × 100 (specimen: 100 % with phenytoin in MES).

## Result

Phenytoin abolished the tonic hind-limb extensor phase in MES seizures and diazepam delayed or prevented PTZ seizures (specimen values), showing anticonvulsant activity.

## Precautions

1. Wet the electrodes with saline for good contact; keep everything else dry.
2. Use the same current and duration for all animals in a group.
3. Do not apply electrodes while the machine is switched on.
4. Observe each PTZ-treated animal in its own cage.
5. Set humane end points in advance and keep suffering to a minimum.

## Viva questions

1. **Which seizure type does MES represent?** Generalised tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizures.
2. **Which seizure type does PTZ represent?** Absence (petit mal) and myoclonic seizures.
3. **What is the end point of protection in MES?** Abolition of the tonic hind-limb extensor phase.
4. **Standard drug for MES?** Phenytoin.
5. **Standard drug for PTZ?** Diazepam (also ethosuximide or valproate).
6. **How does PTZ cause seizures?** By blocking GABA-A receptors and so reducing inhibition.
7. **Why is phenytoin ineffective in PTZ seizures?** It blocks sodium channels and prevents seizure spread, which does not stop PTZ-type (absence-like) seizures.
8. **List the phases of an MES seizure.** Flexion, extensor, clonus, stupor and recovery or death.
practicals.title: Anticonvulsant effect by MES and PTZ methods

# Study of stereotypy and anti-catatonic activity of drugs in rats or mice

**Aim:** To study drug-induced stereotyped behaviour and its blockade by antipsychotics, and drug-induced catatonia (catalepsy) and its reversal by anti-catatonic drugs, in rats or mice.

> Shown by simulation or video as per the PCI note. Live use needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules; set a cut-off time so animals are not held in abnormal postures for long (3Rs, refinement). Use drugs and doses from your lab manual.

## Principle

### A. Stereotypy
Strong stimulation of dopamine receptors in the striatum by **amphetamine** (releases dopamine) or **apomorphine** (direct dopamine agonist) produces repeated, purposeless movements: sniffing, head bobbing, licking, gnawing and biting. These are scored on a rating scale. **Antipsychotics** (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) block D2 receptors and **reduce** the stereotypy score. This is a screening test for antipsychotic activity.

### B. Catatonia (catalepsy)
Blocking D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway with **haloperidol** (or chlorpromazine) makes the animal keep an abnormal posture for a long time – **catalepsy**, a model of drug-induced parkinsonism (extrapyramidal side effects). Drugs that reduce this – **anticholinergics** such as scopolamine, benztropine or trihexyphenidyl, and dopaminergic drugs – show **anti-catatonic activity**.

In the **bar test**, the forepaws of the animal are placed on a horizontal bar raised above the floor; the time it keeps this posture is noted (with a fixed cut-off).

## Requirements

Rats or mice, amphetamine or apomorphine, haloperidol, an anticholinergic (for example scopolamine), vehicle, syringes, balance, observation cages, horizontal bar (catalepsy bar) set at the height in your manual, stopwatch; or simulation software.

## Procedure

### A. Stereotypy
1. Divide animals into a control group (vehicle, then amphetamine/apomorphine) and a test group (antipsychotic, then amphetamine/apomorphine).
2. Give the antipsychotic or vehicle first; after the waiting time, give amphetamine or apomorphine.
3. Place each animal in a separate cage and score stereotyped behaviour at fixed intervals (for example every 10 min for 1 h) using the scale below.

**Example rating scale (follow the scale in your manual):**

| Score | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Normal, asleep or still |
| 1 | Moving about, occasional sniffing |
| 2 | Continuous sniffing and head movements |
| 3 | Continuous sniffing with licking or rearing |
| 4 | Gnawing or biting of the cage bars |

### B. Catatonia and anti-catatonic activity
1. Give haloperidol to two groups. Group I then receives vehicle; Group II receives the anticholinergic (as timed in your manual).
2. At fixed intervals (for example 30, 60, 90 and 120 min after haloperidol), place the forepaws gently on the bar with the hind paws on the floor.
3. Note the time until the animal removes both forepaws (catalepsy time). Stop at the cut-off time (for example 180 s).

## Observations

**Specimen readings – stereotypy score at 30 min (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Group | Animal 1 | Animal 2 | Animal 3 | Mean score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vehicle + amphetamine | 4 | 3 | 4 | 3.7 |
| Haloperidol + amphetamine | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0.7 |

**Specimen readings – catalepsy (bar) time at 60 min, cut-off 180 s (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Group | Animal 1 (s) | Animal 2 (s) | Animal 3 (s) | Mean (s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Haloperidol + vehicle | 180 | 165 | 180 | 175 |
| Haloperidol + scopolamine | 35 | 20 | 40 | 31.7 |

## Result

The antipsychotic reduced amphetamine-induced stereotypy, and the anticholinergic reduced haloperidol-induced catatonia, showing anti-catatonic activity (specimen values).

## Precautions

1. Score behaviour at the same times for all animals, preferably without knowing the group (blind scoring).
2. Keep one animal per cage while scoring.
3. Place the forepaws on the bar gently; do not force the animal.
4. Use a fixed cut-off time in the bar test.
5. Keep the room quiet and evenly lit.

## Viva questions

1. **What is stereotypy?** Repeated, purposeless movements such as sniffing, licking and gnawing caused by strong dopamine stimulation.
2. **Name two drugs that cause stereotypy.** Amphetamine and apomorphine.
3. **Why do antipsychotics reduce stereotypy?** They block D2 dopamine receptors.
4. **What is catalepsy?** A state in which the animal keeps an imposed abnormal posture for a long time.
5. **Which drug is used to produce catalepsy?** Haloperidol.
6. **Clinical meaning of catalepsy in animals?** It predicts extrapyramidal (parkinsonism-like) side effects of antipsychotics.
7. **Name an anti-catatonic drug.** Scopolamine, benztropine or trihexyphenidyl (anticholinergics).
8. **Why do anticholinergics reduce catatonia?** D2 blockade leaves striatal cholinergic activity unopposed; anticholinergics restore the balance.
practicals.title: Stereotypy and anti-catatonic activity in rats/mice

# Study of anxiolytic activity of drugs using rats or mice

**Aim:** To study the anxiolytic (anti-anxiety) activity of a drug in rats or mice using the elevated plus maze.

> Shown by simulation or video as per the PCI note. Live use needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules; each animal is tested only once on the maze, so plan group sizes carefully (3Rs). Use the drug and dose from your lab manual.

## Principle

Rodents naturally avoid open, raised spaces and prefer enclosed spaces. The **elevated plus maze** has two open arms and two closed (walled) arms in a plus shape, raised above the floor. A normal animal spends most of its time in the closed arms. An **anxiolytic** such as **diazepam** reduces this fear, so the animal **enters the open arms more often and spends more time in them**.

```text
                  closed arm (walls)
                        ||
     open arm  ======== [ ] ========  open arm
                        ||
                  closed arm (walls)
            (whole maze raised above the floor)
```

**% open-arm entries = Open-arm entries ÷ (Open + Closed entries) × 100**
**% time in open arms = Time in open arms ÷ (Time in open + closed arms) × 100**

Other anxiety models: light–dark box, open field, hole-board, social interaction test.

## Requirements

Elevated plus maze (dimensions as in your manual), rats or mice, diazepam, vehicle, syringes, balance, stopwatch or video tracking, dilute alcohol for cleaning; or simulation software.

## Procedure

1. Divide animals into a control (vehicle) group and a test (diazepam) group.
2. Give the vehicle or drug (usually intraperitoneally) and wait for the time in your manual (for example 30 min).
3. Place each animal in the centre of the maze facing an open arm.
4. For a fixed period (commonly 5 min) record:
   - number of entries into open arms and closed arms (an entry = all four paws inside the arm);
   - time spent in open and closed arms.
5. Remove the animal, clean the maze, and test the next one.
6. Calculate % open-arm entries and % time in open arms.

## Observations and calculation

**Specimen readings for a 5-min test (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Group | Animal | Open-arm entries | Closed-arm entries | % open entries | Time open (s) | Time closed (s) | % time open |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | 1 | 2 | 10 | 16.7 | 25 | 240 | 9.4 |
| | 2 | 3 | 9 | 25.0 | 35 | 225 | 13.5 |
| Diazepam | 1 | 7 | 8 | 46.7 | 110 | 150 | 42.3 |
| | 2 | 8 | 7 | 53.3 | 125 | 140 | 47.2 |

Worked example (Control animal 1): % open entries = 2 ÷ (2 + 10) × 100 = 16.7 %.

## Result

Diazepam increased the percentage of open-arm entries and time spent in the open arms, showing anxiolytic activity (specimen values).

## Precautions

1. Test each animal only once on the maze; repeat exposure changes behaviour.
2. Clean the maze between animals to remove smell cues.
3. Keep light, noise and time of day the same for all animals.
4. The observer should sit still and away from the maze, or use video.
5. Note any fall from an open arm and exclude that animal as per the manual.

## Viva questions

1. **Principle of the elevated plus maze?** Natural fear of open, raised spaces; anxiolytics increase exploration of the open arms.
2. **Standard anxiolytic used?** Diazepam.
3. **Mechanism of diazepam?** It increases the frequency of GABA-A chloride channel opening in response to GABA.
4. **What counts as an arm entry?** All four paws inside the arm.
5. **Name two other anxiety models.** Light–dark box and open field test.
6. **Why is each animal tested only once?** Prior exposure reduces open-arm exploration and makes the test insensitive.
7. **What would an anxiogenic drug do?** Reduce open-arm entries and time.
practicals.title: Anxiolytic activity using the elevated plus maze

# Study of local anaesthetics by different methods

**Aim:** To study the action of local anaesthetics by surface, infiltration and nerve-block (conduction) methods.

> Shown by simulation or video as per the PCI note. Live use needs IAEC approval under CPCSEA rules and the 3Rs; frogs and guinea pigs are no longer used for routine teaching. Use the drug strengths in your lab manual.

## Principle

Local anaesthetics (lignocaine, procaine, bupivacaine, tetracaine) block voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve membranes, so nerve impulses cannot start or travel along the nerve. Sensation is lost in the area supplied, while the animal stays conscious. Their action can be tested in three ways:

| Method | Type of anaesthesia | Animal | Test of sensation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Corneal reflex method | Surface (topical) | Rabbit | Blink when the cornea is touched |
| Intradermal wheal method | Infiltration | Guinea pig | Skin twitch to a pin prick on the wheal |
| Foot withdrawal (plexus) method | Nerve block (conduction) | Frog | Withdrawal of the foot dipped in dilute acid |

Other methods: tail nerve block in mice or rats, and spinal (intrathecal) anaesthesia in rabbits.

## Requirements

Local anaesthetic solutions (for example lignocaine, procaine), normal saline as control, rabbit holder, cotton wisp, syringes with fine needles, electric clipper, marker pen, pin, frog board, beaker of dilute HCl, beaker of water, stopwatch; or simulation software.

## Procedure

### A. Surface anaesthesia – rabbit cornea
1. Test the corneal reflex in both eyes by touching the cornea from the side with a cotton wisp.
2. Put a few drops of the local anaesthetic into one eye and saline into the other.
3. Test the reflex every minute; note the time when the blink is lost (onset) and when it returns (duration).

### B. Infiltration anaesthesia – guinea pig intradermal wheal
1. Clip the hair on the back a day before.
2. Inject a small volume of the anaesthetic intradermally to raise a wheal; mark it. Inject saline on the other side as control.
3. Prick the wheal with a pin a fixed number of times (for example 6) at regular intervals (for example every 5 min for 30 min).
4. Count the pricks that give **no** skin twitch. More "no response" counts mean stronger anaesthesia.

### C. Nerve block – frog foot withdrawal
1. Pith the frog (brain only, so spinal reflexes remain) and suspend it on a stand.
2. Dip one foot in dilute HCl; note the time taken to withdraw it. Wash the foot in water at once.
3. Put the anaesthetic solution into the abdominal lymph sac so that it reaches the lumbar nerve plexus.
4. Repeat the acid test at fixed intervals; note when the foot is no longer withdrawn within a fixed cut-off time (onset of nerve block).

## Observations

**Specimen readings – surface anaesthesia (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Eye | Drug | Onset (loss of corneal reflex, min) | Duration (min) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Right | Lignocaine | 2 | 22 |
| Left | Saline | No loss | – |

**Specimen readings – intradermal wheal, 6 pricks per test (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Time (min) | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30 | Total no-response (of 36) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Saline | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Lignocaine | 6 | 6 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 30 |

**Specimen readings – frog foot withdrawal, cut-off 15 s (illustrative only, not real data):**

| Time after drug (min) | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Withdrawal time (s) | 3 | 6 | 15 (no withdrawal) | 15 (no withdrawal) |

## Result

The local anaesthetic produced surface, infiltration and conduction anaesthesia; onset and duration were noted (specimen values) and saline had no effect.

## Precautions

1. Touch the cornea from the side so the animal does not blink at the approaching object.
2. Inject strictly intradermally, raising a clear wheal; deep injection gives false results.
3. Use the same pin pressure for every prick.
4. Wash the frog's foot in water immediately after each acid test.
5. Always run a saline control.

## Viva questions

1. **Mechanism of action of local anaesthetics?** They block voltage-gated sodium channels and stop nerve conduction.
2. **Which method tests surface anaesthesia?** The rabbit corneal reflex method.
3. **Which animal is used for the intradermal wheal method?** The guinea pig.
4. **Why is adrenaline added to some local anaesthetic injections?** It constricts blood vessels, slowing absorption so the action lasts longer and systemic toxicity is lower.
5. **Which nerve fibres are blocked first?** Small fibres carrying pain and temperature before large motor fibres.
6. **Name an ester and an amide local anaesthetic.** Procaine (ester) and lignocaine (amide).
7. **Why is only the brain destroyed in the frog?** The spinal reflex arc must work for the withdrawal reflex.
8. **Why is procaine poor as a surface anaesthetic?** It penetrates mucous membranes poorly.
practicals.title: Local anaesthetics by different methods

questions.answer:
1. Definition: chemical alteration of a drug in the body, mainly in liver microsomes, making it more polar and water-soluble for excretion.
2. Results: active → inactive (most drugs); active → active metabolite (diazepam → desmethyldiazepam, codeine → morphine); prodrug → active (levodopa → dopamine, enalapril → enalaprilat); drug → toxic metabolite (paracetamol → NAPQI).
3. Phase I (functionalisation): oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4, 2D6, 2C9) — the commonest; reduction (chloramphenicol); hydrolysis of esters and amides (procaine, succinylcholine by plasma esterases); cyclisation/decyclisation. Adds or exposes −OH, −NH2, −COOH.
4. Phase II (conjugation): glucuronidation (commonest: morphine, paracetamol, chloramphenicol), acetylation (isoniazid, sulfonamides, hydralazine; slow/fast acetylators), sulfation, methylation (adrenaline), glycine conjugation (salicylic acid), glutathione conjugation (NAPQI). Products usually inactive and water-soluble.
5. Hofmann elimination: atracurium breaks down spontaneously in plasma.
6. Enzyme induction: phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin, griseofulvin, chronic alcohol, smoking increase enzyme synthesis over days; consequences — oral contraceptive failure with rifampicin, reduced warfarin effect, autoinduction (carbamazepine); use — phenobarbitone in neonatal jaundice.
7. Enzyme inhibition: cimetidine, erythromycin, ketoconazole, ciprofloxacin, valproate, allopurinol, grapefruit juice; quick onset; toxicity of other drugs (erythromycin + theophylline; ketoconazole + terfenadine arrhythmia).
8. Clinical note: newborns have poor glucuronidation → grey baby syndrome with chloramphenicol.
